options.text: It aims to satisfy victims by guaranteeing the offender performs public service work.

questions.explanation: Negotiated justice aims at reduced reoffending by changing the offender's behaviour, not merely punishing the past. Harsher punishment, court cost savings and symbolic reparation each miss that behavioural aim.

questions.explanation: A collective right attaches to the group and is exercised through a body that speaks for it. Personal claims, state ownership and the exclusion of individuals each misdescribe that category.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret an extract stating the duty to bring trials promptly

stimulus.body: A regional court act states that criminal trials shall be brought without unreasonable delay, that the delay shall be judged against the complexity of the case, and that the burden of explaining an undue delay rests on the authority bringing the charge. options.text: The court must schedule every criminal trial within a fixed number of days set by the statute.
options.misconception: mistakes a flexible standard for a rigid deadline

options.text: The court must postpone any complex case until every possible line of inquiry is complete.
options.misconception: reads the complexity factor as an unlimited excuse for delay

questions.explanation: The excerpt imposes a duty to bring trials without unreasonable delay, with the burden of explaining delay on the charge. Fixed deadlines, blanket postponement and blanket excuses each distort it.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why identical formal designs can yield different results
questions.stem: Dew on the lens, 11 September: a report compares a reform that works in one region with a stalled reform elsewhere; explain in what sense the design of a justice reform does not by itself determine its results.

answer.exemplar: A reform's design sets its formal structure, but its results depend on how that structure is used in practice: local courts may apply new sentencing rules inconsistently, budget shortfalls may leave new posts empty, and staff may lack training. Design is therefore a necessary input whose effects are filtered through implementation capacity and local conditions, which is why the same design yields different results across regions.

questions.explanation: The prompt asks for a written account of how formal design interacts with implementation. A strong answer links design to local capacity, training and resources rather than treating the written rule as self-executing.
questions.hint: Separate the written rule from the conditions of its use.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Set out a method for separating design from practice in reform
questions.stem: Dew on the lens, 17 November: a regional office is told to explain how a new sentencing guideline produced unexpected local effects; explain how design and practice should be separated in that assessment.

answer.exemplar: A sound explanation would separate the guideline's formal design, its stated aims and its internal consistency from the way courts, defence lawyers and offenders actually use it, and would then test which local conditions, such as court list pressure, lack of training or altered sentencing guidance, could produce the observed effects. It should also acknowledge limits, such as small numbers and the absence of a comparison group, and avoid treating the guideline's design as either wholly responsible or wholly irrelevant.

questions.explanation: The prompt asks for a written method for separating formal design from practical operation. A strong answer identifies implementation conditions and evidential limits rather than assigning sole responsibility to the rule's text.
questions.hint: Separate what the rule says from how it is used.

answer.exemplar: The diagnosis should start by testing the rule itself for clarity, internal consistency and workable drafting, then test the practice for evidence of misunderstanding, evasion or capacity failure. stimulus.body: The appellate court notes that the defendant waited nineteen months for trial, that the first listing was postponed because the courtroom was reassigned, that a further four months passed before a date was confirmed, and that the defendant had meanwhile remained on remand. The court holds that the delay was not justified and that the state must answer for the consequences, while making no observation about whether the delay was intended to disadvantage the defendant.

questions.stem: Seeing steady tonight, 18 January: given the extract, which option best captures what the appellate court has established?

options.text: The court established that the delay was caused deliberately in order to prejudice the defendant.
options.misconception: reads a finding of unreasonableness as a finding of intent

options.text: The court established that the delay was unjustified and that the state must meet its consequences.
The court established that the courtroom reassignment was an acceptable administrative reason.
options.misconception: reinstates a justification the excerpt rejects

options.text: The court established that the defendant's remand was lawful throughout the period of waiting.
options.misconception: assumes a separate legality ruling that was not made

questions.explanation: The excerpt establishes that the delay was unjustified and the state must answer for it, finding no intent. Deliberate prejudice, administrative acceptability and a remand ruling overstate.
questions.hint: Note what the court found and what it left open.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: State the definition of complementarity
questions.stem: Notebook entry, 26 February: a student defines complementarity as the relationship between international supervision and national justice systems; what is the definition?

options.text: National systems bear primary responsibility, and international bodies act where national protection fails.
International bodies bear primary responsibility, and national courts act only where they are permitted.
options.misconception: inverts which level bears primary responsibility

options.text: Both levels share identical competence in every case, with no priority given to either.
options.misconception: claims an identity of competence that the concept denies

options.text: International bodies replace national courts whenever the two hold different views of a case.
options.misconception: confuses the concept with unilateral replacement

questions.explanation: Complementarity means states remain primarily responsible for rights, and international supervision covers national failures. Inverted responsibility and unilateral replacement misstate the term.
questions.hint: Remember who holds primary responsibility under the concept.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Set out how to compare two similar statutes on compliance
questions.stem: Dew on the lens, 10 March: a study compares how two statutes with similar wording produced different compliance; explain how design and practice should be separated in that comparison.

answer.exemplar: The comparison should begin with the two statutes themselves, checking whether wording that appears similar is in fact identical in scope, exceptions and sanction, because differences in design would explain divergent compliance directly. If the designs are effectively the same, the analysis then turns to practice: local guidance, training, monitoring and the informal norms of each field office. The account should also state what the comparison cannot establish, such as whether formal compliance in one setting was achieved through substantive or merely procedural conformity.

questions.explanation: The prompt asks for a written account of how to separate textual design from practical operation. A strong answer checks whether the wording really matches before attributing divergence to local practice.
questions.hint: Check the texts first, then look at local practice.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the guiding consideration for procedural simplification
questions.stem: Telescope log, 21 April: a proposal moves small claims to a single adjudicator rather than a panel; what consideration should drive the assessment?

options.text: Whether the change will attract more professional litigants, since volume often signals appeal.
options.misconception: reads volume of use as evidence of appeal confidence

options.text: Whether the change will reduce the number of claims filed, which is the usual reform aim.
options.misconception: assumes deterrence of claims is the reform objective

options.text: Whether the streamlined process still delivers a hearing that parties can understand and trust.
Whether the adjudicator will be elected locally, since local accountability improves decisions.
options.misconception: invents an election requirement no proposal mentions

questions.explanation: A streamlined process must still deliver a hearing litigants understand and trust, so comprehension and fairness guide assessment. Volume, deterrence of claims and local elections are not at issue.
questions.hint: Ask whether a faster hearing is still a fair hearing.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Compute and interpret the share of successful appeals
questions.stem: Sky notes, 6 May: a reform is evaluated with the figures 900 appeals, 380 allowed and 70 remitted; which option best describes the result?

options.text: Fewer than half of the appeals that reached a decision were successful, so the appeal route fails.
options.misconception: treats a success rate under half as proof of failure

options.text: The reform succeeded in 50 per cent of cases, which is a clear improvement on earlier years.
options.misconception: invents a comparison with earlier years from a single dataset

options.text: Remitted cases should be excluded, since a case sent back proves nothing about the appeal.
options.misconception: excludes a genuine category of successful appeal

options.text: 450 of 900 appeals ended successfully, 380 by substitution and 70 by remittal.

questions.explanation: 380 allowed plus 70 remitted gives 450 of 900 successful appeals, so half succeeded, substitution the larger route. Excluding remittals and invented comparisons each misread the data.
questions.hint: Add the two kinds of successful outcome.
